node.label: David Arnold
node.description: A historian of South Asia, and a founding member of the Subaltern Studies collective, whose work brings medicine, science and environment into the study of colonial power. Colonizing the Body (1993) studies state medicine and epidemic disease in nineteenth-century India. The introduction to Science, Technology and Medicine in Colonial India (2000) rejects a single trajectory from European discovery to passive reception overseas. Drawing on Steven Shapin’s account of knowledge as socially situated, it insists that a history of science in India must also be a history of India. It criticizes George Basalla’s diffusion model for flattening differences among colonial situations, marginalizing local agency and assuming a beneficial sequence of development, while also rejecting accounts that understate colonial disruption. His environmental histories include The Problem of Nature (1996) and The Tropics and the Traveling Gaze (2006).
